analysis.one_liner: Creates a temporary federal backstop so insurers keep covering losses from major terrorist attacks.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed it 84-14 on June 18, 2002, and folded it into H.R. 3210, which became the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act of 2002.
analysis.plain_summary: After the September 11 attacks, insurers began dropping or dramatically repricing terrorism coverage, which threatened construction projects, commercial real estate deals, and business lending that depend on property insurance. This bill forces insurance companies to offer terrorism coverage and creates a federal program that pays 80 to 90 percent of catastrophic terrorism losses above industry deductibles, up to a $100 billion annual cap. It also creates a single federal lawsuit channel for terrorism victims, replacing state court claims, and lets judgments against state sponsors of terrorism be paid from their frozen U.S. assets.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses, landlords, and homeowners who need property insurance, and construction and real estate projects that lenders will not finance without terrorism coverage. Insurance companies also benefit: the federal government absorbs most losses above their deductibles and caps their liability at $100 billion per year.

how_it_helps.text: Mandates that every participating insurer make terrorism coverage available in its property and casualty policies, on terms no worse than coverage for other disasters, so policyholders cannot be stranded after an attack [S3][S4].

Has the Treasury pay 80 percent of insured terrorism losses between the industry deductibles and $10 billion, and 90 percent above that, so premiums for terrorism coverage stay affordable rather than spiking unpredictably [S3][S4].

Keeps construction, property purchases, and business interruption protection moving after an attack; the bill's own findings state that insurers withdrawing or repricing terrorism coverage would suppress construction, raise rents, and stall economic activity [S4].

Guarantees victims of terrorism a federal cause of action and lets them satisfy judgments from frozen assets of terrorists and state sponsors of terrorism, with a special payment rule for judgments against Iran [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who quietly take on the risk of up to $100 billion in terrorism losses per year; terrorism victims, whose state-law lawsuits are preempted by the federal cause of action; and potentially future taxpayers if the temporary program is extended rather than retired.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, and victims whose state suits are preempted

drawbacks.text: Taxpayers bear 80 to 90 percent of catastrophic terrorism losses up to $100 billion a year while insurers keep the premiums they collect for terrorism coverage, with only a market-share deductible offsetting the federal exposure [S3][S4].

The bill preempts all state causes of action for property damage, personal injury, or death from terrorism, making the federal claim the exclusive remedy except against the terrorists themselves, which narrows victims' ability to sue under state law [S4].
The Treasury Secretary's decisions on what counts as an act of terrorism and whether to extend the program are final and cannot be reviewed by any court [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The immediate problem this solved was real: lenders and developers were freezing deals because insurers would not quote terrorism coverage. The trade-off is that the program socializes the tail risk — insurers keep collecting premiums while taxpayers stand behind the largest losses — and its one-year sunset with a discretionary extension, decided by Treasury alone, gave the industry a path to ask for more. For terrorism victims, guaranteed compensation came bundled with the loss of state-court remedies.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it 84-14, then a week later folded it into the House's version of the same bill, H.R. 3210, which was enacted as the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act of 2002.

narrative.text: After September 11, insurers were excluding terrorism coverage or sharply raising prices, and Congress found this could stall construction and suppress economic activity [S4].
The Senate took the bill up within days of introduction: it was laid before the Senate by unanimous consent on June 13 and a cloture motion was filed June 14 [S6].
Cloture — the vote needed to cut off debate and move to final passage — was invoked 65-31 on June 18, with 47 of 50 Senate Democrats in favor and 30 of 49 Senate Republicans opposed [S6][S7].
The Senate passed the amended bill 84-14 the same day: every Senate Democrat present voted yes, and 34 of 49 Senate Republicans joined them [S6][S8].
The Senate incorporated the measure into H.R. 3210, the House vehicle, on July 25, 2002 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurance companies gained a federal backstop for their largest terrorism losses, and businesses and builders regained access to affordable terrorism coverage.

for.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
for.role: Senator from Connecticut and lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it to Senate passage in eleven days.

for.name: President George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Pushed Congress to enact a federal terrorism insurance backstop after September 11.

against.name: 30 of 49 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against the cloture motion to end debate, though most ultimately voted for the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Democrats were unanimous in favor; Republicans split, with 34 of 49 voting for passage after 30 of 49 first voted against cutting off debate.

industries.note: The bill forces insurers to keep selling terrorism coverage, which protects policyholders, but the federal government then pays 80-90 percent of losses above insurer deductibles up to $100 billion while insurers keep the premiums — a taxpayer backstop the industry had sought since September 11.

industries.industry: Commercial real estate, construction, and lenders
industries.note: These businesses depend on property insurance for financing; restored terrorism coverage keeps projects and transactions viable, which the bill's findings tie directly to construction and rents.
Taxpayers assume the risk of up to $100 billion in terrorism losses per year, an exposure that grows if the one-year program is extended.
By making a single federal cause of action the exclusive remedy, the bill removes victims' state-law claims, limiting the lawsuits such defendants could face.
